Where do renters live in Vancouver?

The Tenant Commons map shows rental buildings: who owns, manages and licenses them. The 2021 census counted renter households in Vancouver, and the City's SRO inventory another rooms the census leaves out. On this page, we account for them piece by piece: first the buildings the map shows, then the homes it doesn't try to show, and at the end what no record explains.


Scroll to read; pick a neighbourhood above the map, or click one on it, to see its own numbers.

Start

All households

households in in the 2021 census, of which rent.

The bar above the map shows all households, renters filled in. Renting isn't spread evenly: Downtown, the West End and Fairview are mostly renters; the single-family west side and the southeast mostly own. The map shades each neighbourhood by the share of households who rent.

How we know

Statistics Canada, 2021 Census of Population, profile by dissemination area: private households by tenure. Tenure comes from the long-form questionnaire (a 25% sample), so each small area's figure carries a margin of a few dozen households; summed over a neighbourhood that averages out to a few percent.

Neighbourhoods are the City of Vancouver's 22 local areas.

The number to account for

renter homes

From here on the bar is renter homes only, and it starts empty. Each of the next sections fills in one piece, in one colour used everywhere: on the bar, on the map and in the text. The line in the panel keeps the running total.

The labels on the map are each neighbourhood's renter homes.

How we know

Same census table as above. A "household" is the people living in one private dwelling; the census counts households, the map counts units, so the two need converting (see "Non-market housing and co-ops"). SRO rooms are counted as rooms.

On the map · piece 1 of 3

Purpose-built rental

households in market rental buildings the map shows

Apartment buildings built or run as rentals. Each dot is a building, sized by its units.

of these households live in buildings on the City's rental list.

, or , live in buildings the City's list doesn't include. The map finds them through their rental business licence, whose fee shows how many units they have. Most are larger buildings: established rentals licensed since at least 2013, and newer ones built since 2011. They're the lighter blue part of the bar and the lighter blue dots.

Hollow grey dots are buildings finished after the census: on the map, but they can't be in a 2021 count, so they go on the grey track under the bar.

Buildings outside are greyed out.

The map's coverage holds up against the national count. CMHC's rental survey counted units in purpose-built rental buildings of six or more units in October 2021. The map has units in buildings of that size, including the ones known only from their licence: about a tenth more, not less. It also has units in 3–5 unit buildings (mostly converted houses in Kitsilano, Mount Pleasant and along East Hastings) that CMHC doesn't survey.

How we know

Map buildings: the Tenant Commons build (City of Vancouver Open Data: rental licences, property tax roll; FOI 2024-698 purpose-built rental list). Units are counted as households using each census area's occupancy rate (occupied ÷ total dwellings).

Licence-only buildings were dated from the tax roll's improvement values (2020–2026) and their rental licences since 2013: a building whose improvements appear after 2021, or that was first licensed after the census, came after it. Where the tax roll has no record (no match, or demolished since), the licences decide. The roll's year built is unreliable on redeveloped sites.

CMHC Rental Market Survey, October 2021, universe by census tract (HMIP table 2.1.26.6). Buildings finished after the census are left out of both sides.

On the map · piece 2 of 3

Non-market housing and co-ops

households in non-market, social and co-op housing

Social housing run by non-profits and BC Housing, City-owned rentals, and housing co-ops. Co-op members are counted as renters by the census, so they belong in the count. Non-market buildings finished after the census are hollow grey too: in all, units on the map came after the census.

more non-profit buildings, mostly shelters and supportive housing, hold a rental licence that doesn't say how many units they have. They're drawn as small dots but add nothing to the count.

Units aren't households. Across purpose-built and non-market housing the map has units, but on census day some stood empty or between tenants. Using each area's occupancy, that's households: of renter homes.

How we know

City of Vancouver non-market housing list (Open Data), CHF BC's co-op directory, and buildings on City-owned land. Same occupancy conversion as above.

Occupancy: occupied ÷ total private dwellings in each census area, capped at 1.

On the map · piece 3 of 3

SRO hotels and rooming houses

rooms in SRO hotels and rooming houses, counted in the bar and added to the total

Single-room-occupancy hotels are some of the city's most important low-cost housing, and the map shows every one. The census doesn't count their tenants as renter households: it files rooming houses and residential hotels as "collective dwellings", like care homes and shelters, whose residents have no tenure. In the census's renter count, SRO tenants don't exist.

This page counts them. Their rooms are added to the total and to the pieces alike, so the bar holds every rented home the census and the City's SRO inventory know of. A room isn't a household: some stand empty or closed, and a few SRO tenants were counted by the census after all (see how we know). The difference at the end doesn't change; only its share does.

With SRO rooms, the map shows of renter homes: . That is the map's share.

How we know

Statistics Canada's census dictionary lists lodging or rooming houses and hotels as collective dwellings. The numbers agree: in the 21 census areas with 150 or more SRO rooms,

SRO rooms on the map6,766
census renter households7,385
other rentals on the map5,500
renter households left1,885
condos (about 40% rented: ~2,000)5,020
people in collective dwellings4,231

The renter households left over are about what rented condos explain, leaving no room for SRO tenants, while 4,231 people there live in collective dwellings. Caveats: collective dwellings also include shelters and some supportive housing, and a few SROs look to have been counted as private dwellings (two areas with about 280 and 330 rooms and no collective population).

Sources: City of Vancouver SRO inventory (FOI); 2021 census profile, population and persons in private households.

Not on the map, as expected · piece 1 of 2

Suites, houses and semis

renter households in basement suites, rented houses and semis, estimated

Basement and laneway suites (), whole houses () and semi-detached homes (). They're rented one at a time by whoever owns the house, so they aren't on the map, and aren't expected to be.

How we know

The census counts each area's dwellings by type. City-wide, it says what share of each type is rented (suites in houses 42%, houses 23%, semis 29%; Statistics Canada table 98-10-0240-01). Those rates are applied in every neighbourhood: a simplification that matters in the last section.

Not on the map, as expected · piece 2 of 2

Rented condos

renter households in condos, estimated

Many renters live in condos owned by one person and rented out unit by unit. Like suites, they're rented one at a time: the map tracks buildings and their owners, not individual condo landlords, so these homes aren't on it. Shading shows rented condos as a share of each neighbourhood's renters.

The estimate uses CMHC's count of rented condos, and it may run a little low. Across Metro Vancouver the census finds more condos rented than CMHC does: 37% against 29%. Using the census's rate would add about renter households in . In Vancouver, though, the census's own renter count leaves little room for them (see how we know).

How we know

The census counts condo households in each area. CMHC's condo survey says what share of condo apartments are rented: 48% on the downtown peninsula, 29–30% elsewhere in the city (October 2021). The two measure different things: CMHC counts rented units among all condo units, empty ones included; the census asks the households living in them.

Where there are almost no suites or houses, nearly all renters the map doesn't show live in condos, so the census implies its own rate. It lands close to CMHC's, not above it:

CMHCcensus implies
Downtown47%50%
Mount Pleasant30%30%
Fairview29%26%

Downtown is the one place it hints CMHC runs a few points low. The census's condo count itself is sound: it is close to the tax roll's strata units (111,200 against 116,300 City-wide).

What's left

Census count versus the pieces

City-wide the pieces and the census agree to within about : the totals reconcile. Neighbourhood by neighbourhood they don't, and the difference runs both ways.

Each neighbourhood's difference, as a share of its renter homes. Click a name, or a neighbourhood on the map, to see its ledger.

Several sit right on the 5% line: . A difference that small can come from the estimates themselves. The clear cases are .

Census counts more renters than the pieces. In , the census finds renter households that no building on the map, no condo estimate and no suite estimate accounts for.

Downtown's difference is small, and fits CMHC's condo rate running a few points low here: the census's own numbers imply 50% of Downtown condos are rented, against CMHC's 47%.

In the east and south, the census also finds apartments that are neither condos nor on the map ( in ), most likely houses split into several suites. This is what is truly missing: renters living in homes no public record lists as rentals.

The pieces add up to more than the census. This happens mostly on the west side: in . That is most likely a limit of the estimates, not extra renters: the city-wide rental rates for suites and houses overstate renting in wealthy single-family neighbourhoods, and small samples add noise. It doesn't mean the map shows too much.

Where there are few houses (the West End, Kitsilano and Grandview-Woodland), the suite rates can't be the reason; there it's most likely the condo estimate. CMHC's share of condos rented (48% on the downtown peninsula, 29–30% elsewhere) is an average over large areas and may run high for these neighbourhoods' condos.

How we know

Difference = census renter households − every counted piece above. Positive means the census counts more than the pieces (renters not accounted for); negative means the pieces add up to more than the census (the estimates overshoot). Shading is the difference as a share of the neighbourhood's renters; under 5% either way reads as about even.

Unmapped apartments: census apartments (in buildings of any size) minus condos minus the map's apartment units, per area, never below zero.
